subtitle: Turn small sensor resistance changes into a clean differential voltage
takeaways: A bridge removes the constant part, leaves only the change
Unequal arms (m ≫ 1): less signal, much better linearity
Read the bridge differentially: buffers + difference amp

slides.title: Two dividers, one difference
bullets: V_{d} = V_{A} − V_{B}: difference of two divider taps, neither at ground
Balanced (V_{d} = 0) independent of V_{B}: supply drift cancels at balance
Null method: adjust a known R until V_{d} = 0 (classic Wheatstone)
Deflection method: fixed R, balanced at the reference point, measure V_{d}

falstad.name: wheatstone
falstad.hint: Move the Rx slider: 1010 Ω gives 12.44 mV, 1500 Ω gives 0.500 V

slides.notes: Start from the sensor in a plain divider: the tiny change sits on a large constant voltage. The second divider subtracts that constant part. Away from balance V_d is proportional to V_B, so the excitation must be stable or the measurement ratiometric. Exercise 5.1 does the numbers.

slides.title: Quarter bridge: the output bends
bullets: One sensor R_{0}(1+x), other arms R_{0}: V_{d} = (V_{B}/4)·x/(1+x/2)
Relative error of the linear formula ≈ −x/2
Strain gauge (x < 0.5 %): negligible; Pt100 over 100 K (x = 38.5 %): 16 %
Cause: the current in the sensor leg changes with the sensor
slides.notes: Show the plot: positive x gives too small an output, negative x too large. The derivation is in section Output Voltage and Linearity of the script.

slides.title: Sensitivity vs. linearity: choose m

left.head: Equal arms (m = 1)
bullets: Max. sensitivity V_{B}/4 per unit x
Nonlinearity ≈ −x/2
High sensor current, self-heating

right.head: Unequal arms (m = 39)
bullets: Sensitivity m/(m+1)^{2} = 0.024
Nonlinearity ≈ −x/(m+1): 20× smaller
Sensor leg acts like a current source

slides.notes: R1 = R3 = m·R0. A large m keeps the leg current nearly constant, so the sensor voltage is nearly proportional to its resistance. The amplifier needs gain anyway, while nonlinearity would need software correction.

slides.section: Half and Full Bridges: Strain Gauges
slides.title: Quarter, half, full bridge
bullets: Quarter: 1 gauge, V_{d} ≈ V_{B}·x/4, slightly nonlinear
Half: 2 gauges in adjacent arms, V_{d} = V_{B}·x/2, linear
Full: 4 gauges, V_{d} = V_{B}·x, linear, most signal
slides.rule: x = ΔR/R = k·ε, gauge factor k ≈ 2
slides.notes: Gauges on top of a bending beam are stretched, on the bottom compressed; put them in adjacent arms. The leg current stays constant in half and full bridges, so they are linear. In a quarter bridge a dummy gauge gives the temperature compensation. Half and full bridge: temperature changes all gauges equally and cancels.

slides.section: Half and Full Bridges: Strain Gauges
slides.title: Example: 350 Ω gauges, ε = 1000 µm/m, V_{B} = 5 V
bullets: Quarter 2.50 mV, half 5.00 mV, full 10.0 mV
Gain for 2 V: quarter 800, half 400, full 200
Use: quarter for one sensor (Pt100), half on a bending beam, full in load cells
slides.rule: Twice the active gauges, twice the signal

falstad.name: bridge_types
falstad.hint: Compare the three voltmeters: 2.50 mV, 5.00 mV, 10.0 mV

slides.notes: Top gauges stretched (R2, R3: R(1+x)), bottom compressed (R1, R4: R(1−x)). Stretched gauges go into one diagonal, compressed into the other, so the effects add. Less gain means less amplified noise and offset. Exercise 5.2.

slides.title: Platinum sensors Pt100 and Pt1000
bullets: Linear model good to 0.4 K over 0 … 100 °C; Callendar–Van Dusen beyond
Self-heating ΔT = E·I^{2}·R: Pt100 ≤ 1 mA, Pt1000 ≤ 0.3 mA
slides.notes: Platinum is stable and standardised (IEC 60751). Self-heating depends on coupling to the medium: 0.1 K/mW in flowing water, about 1 K/mW in still air. Exercise 5.3 has the numbers.

slides.title: Platinum RTD vs. NTC thermistor

left.head: Pt100 / Pt1000
bullets: +0.39 %/K, nearly linear
Standardised, accurate, stable
Needs a bridge and gain

right.head: NTC thermistor
bullets: About −4.4 %/K at 25 °C: 10× more
Strongly nonlinear (exponential)
Cheap; linearise with R or a table

slides.notes: NTC model: R(T) = R25·exp(B·(1/T − 1/T25)), for example 10 kΩ and B = 3950 K. The capstone uses the Pt100 because its characteristic is reproducible.

slides.title: Design recipe: sensor bridge
steps: Excite from the ADC reference (ratiometric): here V_{ref} = 4.00 V
R_{4} = R_{sensor}(T_{min}): V_{d} = 0 at T_{min} (Pt100: R_{4} = 100 Ω)
R_{1} ≥ V_{B}/I_{max} − R_{sensor}, next E-value; R_{3} = R_{1} (here 3.9 kΩ)
Exact V_{d}(T_{max}) and gain G = V_{FS}/V_{d}(T_{max}): 37.18 mV, G = 107.6
Check nonlinearity x/(m+1), self-heating, common mode ≈ V_{B}/(m+1)
slides.notes: This is the design card of the chapter applied to the capstone: Pt100, 0 to 100 °C, at most 1 mA. Sensitivity is about 0.37 mV/K and the self-heating 0.1 mW. Worked out in Exercise 5.4.

slides.title: Falstad: capstone bridge, Pt100 and Pt1000
observe: Pt100, m = 39: almost a straight line, 0.09 mV ≈ 0.24 K off at 50 °C
V_{R} stays at 100 mV: the reference arm is the constant part
Pt1000 at 5 V (m = 4.7): 7× more signal, 1.6 % nonlinearity
slides.notes: With m = 1 the same Pt100 bridge would deviate by 4.4 K. The Pt1000 version is Exercise 5.5: more signal and less gain needed, but almost ten times the self-heating power.

slides.title: Read the bridge differentially
bullets: Both taps sit at ≈ 100 mV (common mode); the signal is their difference
Single-ended gain 107.6 at V_{S}: 10.75 V at 0 °C instead of 0 V
Difference amplifier amplifies V_{S} − V_{R}, rejects V_{CM} if R match
Buffers keep the bridge unloaded; gain stage G_{2} = 10.76 → 0 … 4.00 V

falstad.name: bridge_single_ended
falstad.hint: Output far above 4 V: the constant part is amplified too

slides.notes: Open the single-ended version first and show the huge output, then the buffered difference amplifier. Without buffers the 10 kΩ inputs would load the 97.5 Ω bridge and spoil the common-mode rejection. Details in chapter Operational Amplifiers.

slides.title: Falstad: 50 Hz in series with the sensor

falstad.name: bridge_50hz
falstad.hint: Scope: 4.88 mV amplitude at V_S, 0.52 V at Vout

observe: Series interference changes only V_{S}: differential, not rejected
After G = 107.6: 0.52 V amplitude, about one LSB (0.5 V)
Remedies: twisted pair, shield, short leads, low-pass before the ADC
slides.notes: The sensor loop acts as a transformer winding for the lamp fields. Only interference that reaches both nodes equally is common mode. The filter chapter designs the low-pass that removes it.

slides.title: Falstad: 2-wire vs. 3-wire connection

falstad.name: bridge_3wire
falstad.hint: At 100 Ω: 2-wire 0.975 mV, 3-wire 0 V; then both at 138.5 Ω

observe: 2-wire: 2·R_{L} in series with the Pt100; 1 Ω → 2.6 K error
3-wire: R_{L1} and R_{L2} sit in adjacent arms and cancel at balance
4-wire: current through two leads, sense voltage on the other two
slides.notes: Lead resistance 0.5 Ω per wire. At 100 °C the 3-wire error is only 0.05 K (37.16 instead of 37.18 mV), the 2-wire bridge reads 38.13 mV. Exercise 5.6.
